Subject: Clarifying HIPAA on-call support fee vs upfront capex credit for hybrid residency pilot

Hi Logan,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the hybrid residency pilot looks promising. Procurement asked me to confirm how you treat the ‘HIPAA on-call support’ line item we discussed. Two things they want clarified before we move to PO:

1) Can the on-call support fee (monthly) be converted to an upfront capex-style credit applied against implementation costs? If so, how do you amortize it?
2) For KMS/HSM seats and audit-log retention (30 days vs 365 days), what discounting levers are available if we commit to a 12–24 month throughput/commit?

High-level context: MedCorr wants to avoid a recurring surcharge if we can take a larger upfront credit that reduces implementation capital. We’re also sensitive to long-term unit cost for audit storage — if you have options to push more margin into the first-year capex that’d be ideal.

Can you send a quick sketch of scenarios (on-call-as-monthly vs converted-to-capex-credit, seat vs throughput discount) so I can pass to procurement?

Thanks,
Sam

Sam —

Appreciate the clear ask. Short answer: yes — we can structure the on-call support fee as either a recurring surcharge or convert it to an upfront credit against implementation/one-time onboarding fees. Below are three practical scenarios we usually offer. I’m copying Ben for the pricing detail. Neha will join once we hit the legal/evidence side.

Scenario A — Monthly on-call surcharge (standard):
- On-call support: $6,000/month (HIPAA SLA + 24/7 escalation)
- Audit-log 365d retention add-on: $0.03/GB/month after base allotment
- KMS/HSM seats: $1,500/seat/month
- Pros: lowest upfront cash outlay; flexible to scale down after pilot
- Cons: recurring OpEx increases unit economics long-term

Scenario B — Convert on-call to upfront credit applied to implementation:
- We convert 6 months of the on-call fee into a one-time credit applied to the implementation invoice (example: 6 x $6,000 = $36,000 credit)
- Remaining on-call (post-credit) can be zeroed for first 3 months, then revert to monthly thereafter
- Pros: reduces MedCorr capex burden for go-live; keeps OpEx lower in early months
- Cons: credit amortization tied to invoice timing; less usable against ongoing usage fees (tokens/audit storage)

Scenario C — Capex credit + commit-based discount (best for predictable usage):
- Offer 40% off implementation fee if MedCorr commits to a 12-month throughput/commit at target levels (we’ll define TUs)
- Convert on-call fee into a 12-month amortized credit applied monthly against recurring invoice (e.g., $36k credit spread over 12 months = $3k/mo offset)
- Offer reduced KMS/HSM seat price (e.g., $1,050/seat/month) and 20–30% discount on audit storage for 12 months
- Pros: strongest first-year unit economics; aligns incentives

If you want, Ben can attach a quick spreadsheet with exact numbers and breakpoints so procurement can see the P&L impact across years.

I’ll draft the SOW language that turns the on-call into a credit line if you want to pursue that route.

—Logan
Logan Wright

Hi Sam — following up with the numbers Logan promised. I put together three line-items in the attached spreadsheet (MedCorr_Compliance_Pricing_Scenarios.xlsx) showing ARR/1st-year unit cost implications. Highlights: 

- If you elect Scenario B (6-month credit applied to implementation), 1st-year effective unit cost for audit storage is ~12% higher than Scenario C but MedCorr saves ~$36k cash at go-live.
- Scenario C (12-mo commit + capex credit amortized monthly) reduces first-year token/audit cost by ~18% vs standard, while keeping net cash outflow in month 0 close to parity (we amortize credits over invoice schedule).
- HSM seats: we can offer a stepped seat discount: 0–5 seats = $1,350/mo, 6–15 seats = $1,050/mo, >15 seats = $850/mo (requires 12–24 month commit).

Procurement note: converting an on-call fee into a credit requires two things in the SOW — (1) explicit credit application table and (2) invoice schedule mapping credit burn-down. I’ve drafted sample language in the spreadsheet.

If MedCorr can share an ideal cash/expense profile (e.g., prefer minimal month-0 cash vs prefer lower run-rate), we’ll tailor the amortization period and commit term to match.

Thanks,
Ben Carter
Head of Pricing & Commercial Ops | Redwood Inference

Thanks for the scenarios. A couple of clarifying questions before we can accept an LOI:

1) If we pick Scenario C, can the 40% implementation discount be delivered as a vendor credit line on your invoice (i.e., not an off-book vendor rebate)? Procurement prefers credits to be visible on our invoice rather than a post-hoc rebate.
2) For the audit-log retention discount, does the 20–30% hold if we exceed the committed throughput by 20%? We need an overage protection clause so we don’t lose the discount entirely for small bursts.

Also, is Redwood able to add a line in the SOW that treats the on-call fee credit as contingent on achieving an initial onboarding checklist (milestone-based credit release)? We want the credit release tied to evidence delivery (SOC2 attestation + KMS key transfer).

If you can send a draft SOW showing those items and a clean PO-ready invoice template (with credits displayed), we can circulate to finance and legal.

Quick confirmation from legal/compliance side:

- We can structure the 40% implementation concession as an on-invoice credit (will appear as a line item discount on the implementation invoice). We’ll call it “Implementation Credit — MedCorr Pilot.”
- Overages: we can add a protection clause that preserves the committed discount up to +25% throughput; overage pricing above that tier will be billed at the standard audit-storage rate pro-rated monthly.
- Milestone-based credit release: agreed. SOW will include a three-point release schedule: 30% on KMS key transfer and HSM onboarding, 40% on SOC2 evidence delivery, 30% on full cutover/runbook acceptance. Credits are only released against the implementation invoice per schedule.
